title: Background and Context
content: This story is based on an extract from the book, The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, set in the fictional town of St Petersberg in nineteenth century America. Tom is an orphan who lives with his Aunt Polly, his half-brother, Sid and his cousin Mary.
summary: Historical and literary context of the story.

title: Tom's Dilemma
content: Monday morning found Tom Sawyer miserable. Monday morning always found him so - because it began another week's slow suffering in school. I wish there were no holidays in between ... it just makes going back to school so much more difficult.

title: Seeking Illness
content: Tom lay thinking. It occurred to him that he wished he were sick; then he could stay home. Hmm, am I ill? Is something wrong with me? Yes, I think my stomach is aching ... yes, it is certainly getting more painful!
summary: Tom contemplates his physical state to skip school.

title: The Tooth and the Toe
content: Then he remembered hearing the doctor speaking about a certain illness that laid up a patient for two or three weeks. One could even lose a finger from it. I do have a sore toe. But if Aunt Polly comes to know about the tooth, she will want to pull it out, and that will hurt a lot. Tom decided to hold the tooth in reserve for the present and seek further.
summary: Tom finds a loose tooth but decides to keep it as a backup.

title: The Act of Groaning
content: Tom began groaning with spirit, but Sid slept on unconscious. Tom groaned louder and fancied that he began to feel pain in the toe. Tom was panting with his exertions by this time. He rested a moment and then swelled himself up and fetched a succession of admirable groans.
summary: Tom tries to get Sid's attention through performative groaning.

title: Glossary List
content: colicky: associated with a stomach ache. sore: painful and often, red. feeble: weak. fancied: imagined. reflected: thought. exertions: great efforts that make someone tired. hold in reserve: keep something available for later use. succession: (here) series.
summary: Key word meanings from the chapter.

title: Sid's Awakening
content: Tom was annoyed now. He called Sid loudly and shook him. What is the matter, Tom? Why, what's the matter, Tom? I must call auntie. Don't stir so, Sid, you'll kill me. OHHHHH!
summary: Sid wakes up and reacts to Tom's display.

title: The Dying Act
content: I forgive everybody, Sid. Uhhhh! Tell 'em so, Sid. And Sid, you give my window sash and my cat with one eye to that new girl that's come to town, and tell her – Oh, Tom, you ain't dying, are you?
summary: Tom tries to make his sickness look fatal.

title: Aunt Polly's Intervention
content: Dying! Rubbage! I don't believe it! You, Tom! Tom, what's the matter with you? Oh, auntie, my sore toe's mortified! She laughed a little, then cried a little, then did both together. This restored her somewhat. Tom, what a turn you did give me. Your tooth, indeed! Now you shut up that nonsense and climb out of this.
learning_objective: Understand the conclusion of the trick
summary: Aunt Polly discovers Tom is not really dying.

title: Abstract Nouns
content: Abstract nouns refer to things which we cannot see or touch but only feel. They include feelings, experiences, states, qualities and ideas. Example: Tom was suffering in reality now, so handsomely was his imagination working. Abstract nouns can be formed from verbs or adjectives. Examples: behave -> behaviour, speak -> speech, happy -> happiness. They are often formed by adding a suffix to the verb or adjective. Examples: silly -> silliness, communicate -> communication.
summary: Definitions and formation of abstract nouns.

title: Noun Exercises
content: 1. The scientist's work led to an important discovered. 2. I have the greatest admiration for those who help animals. 3. The doctor prescribed three types of medicines for her ill. 4. I share all my happiness, both happy and sad, with my best friend. 5. The loudspeakers are causing annoyance to everyone in the area. 6. We found the house without any difficulty because of the host's clear directions.

title: Countable and Uncountable Nouns
content: Read this sentence: Mary, get me some silk threads, and a chunk of fire out of the kitchen. Here, the noun threads is countable. You know that countable nouns can be singular or plural. The word fire is an uncountable noun. Language Booster: Not all nouns that end with s are plural countable nouns. Examples: measles, mathematics, billiards.
learning_objective: Differentiate between countable and uncountable nouns
summary: Distinguishing between countable and uncountable nouns.

title: Types of Pronouns
content: Personal pronouns are used in place of the names of people and things. These are I, we, you, he, she, it, they, me, us, him, her and them. Example: It occurred to him that he wished he were sick. Possessive pronouns are used to show ownership and belonging. They are mine, yours, his, hers, ours, its and theirs. Example: The one-eyed cat is his. Reflexive pronouns are used when we want to refer back to the subject of the sentence. They are myself, yourself, himself, herself, oneself, itself, ourselves, yourselves, and themselves. Example: He swelled himself up and fetched a succession of admirable groans.

title: Idiom Practice
content: 1. spill the beans - e. tell a secret. 2. turn over a new leaf - a. change one's way of life to become a better, more responsible person. 3. cost an arm and a leg - d. very expensive. 4. the best of both worlds - c. receiving the benefits of two completely different situations at the same time. 5. not see eye to eye - b. not share the same views as somebody about something.
